arXiv:2607.01582v1 [math.CO] 02 Jul 2026

The analytic properties of Hoggatt triangles

Jianxi Mao Email: maojx@dlut.edu.cn    Wenle Shi Email: shi-wenle@hotmail.com Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116024, P.R. China Corresponding author: Corresponding author.
Abstract

The dd-Hoggatt triangle is a lower triangular matrix whose entries are given by specific minors of Pascal’s triangle formed by consecutive dd rows and dd columns. The cases d=1,2,3d=1,2,3 correspond to Pascal’s triangle, the Narayana triangle, and the Baxter triangle, respectively. In this paper, we present the infinite log-concavity of the row and column sequences, the log-concavity of the sequences along transversals, and the eventual log-convexity of the sequences along rays of the dd-Hoggatt triangle. In addition, we prove the asymptotic normality of the row sequences and total positivity of the dd-Hoggatt triangle.

Keywords: 
Hoggatt triangle, Log-concavity, Log-convexity , Pascal’s triangle
2020 MSC
05A05, 05A15, 15B05, 05A10

1 Introduction

Baxter numbers enumerate Baxter permutations originating in Baxter’s study [2] of fixed points for the composite of commuting functions. By inventing a generating tree for Baxter permutations, Chung et al. [13] presented an explicit expression of the Baxter numbers BnB_{n}. Hoggatt conjectured a simple algorithm to generate the refined Baxter numbers

B⁡(n,k)=(nk)​(n+1k)​(n+2k)(k+1k)​(k+2k),B(n,k)=\frac{\binom{n}{k}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+2}{k}}{\binom{k+1}{k}\binom{k+2}{k}},

where Bn=∑k=0nB⁡(n,k)B_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}B(n,k). Fielder and Alford [17] proved Hoggatt’s conjecture and defined Hoggatt triangles with index dd as a generalization of Pascal’s triangle. The Baxter triangle is the case d=3d=3. It was shown that the entries of the Hoggatt triangle are special minors of Pascal’s triangle, see [26, 14].

Definition 1.1.

Let d≥1d\geq 1. Define the dd-Hoggatt triangle Hd=[Hd​(n,k)]n,k≥0H_{d}=\left[H_{d}(n,k)\right]_{n,k\geq 0} as

Hd​(n,k)=det((n+ik+j))i,j=0d−1.H_{d}(n,k)=\det\left(\binom{n+i}{k+j}\right)_{i,j=0}^{d-1}.

Note that when d=1,2,3d=1,2,3, the dd-Hoggatt triangles correspond to Pascal’s triangle, the Narayana triangle and the Baxter triangle [B⁡(n,k)]n,k≥0\left[B(n,k)\right]_{n,k\geq 0}, respectively. The Hoggatt triangle and the Hoggatt numbers Hd​(n,k)H_{d}(n,k) have many fascinating properties [26, 35, 39, 42]. From an analytic perspective, Dilks [15] proved the row generating functions of Hoggatt triangles have only real zeros. Recently, Fang, Zhang and Zhao [16] established the interlacing property of the row generating functions of the Baxter triangle, a property stronger than polynomial with only real zeros. They also generalized this result to Hoggatt triangles, as a stronger version of Dilks’ result. On the other hand, the analytic properties of Pascal’s triangle have been extensively studied in the literature [22, 28]. For example, Su and Wang [37] and Yu [41] presented the log-behavior of the sequences located in a transversal or a ray of Pascal’s triangle. Zhu [45] showed the Stieltjes moment property of the ray of Pascal’s triangle. However, the log-behavior of sequences in the Narayana triangle and the Baxter triangle has been less studied than that of Pascal’s triangle, see [12, 16]. The aim of this paper is to extend several analytic properties of Pascal’s triangle to the Narayana triangle and the Baxter triangle. We will show that the Hoggatt triangles play an important unifying role in proving these results.

Let α={ak}k=0∞\alpha=\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} be a sequence of nonnegative numbers with no internal zeros. The sequence is said to be log-concave (resp. log-convex) if ak2≥ak−1​ak+1a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k-1}a_{k+1} (resp. ak2≤ak−1​ak+1a_{k}^{2}\leq a_{k-1}a_{k+1}) for all k≥1k\geq 1. The sequence is said to be unimodal if there exists an index nn such that a0≤a1≤⋯≤an−1≤an≥an+1≥⋯a_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq\dots\leq a_{n-1}\leq a_{n}\geq a_{n+1}\geq\cdots or it is an increasing or decreasing sequence. Clearly, log-concavity implies unimodality. Define the operator ℒ\mathcal{L} on the sequence α={ak}k=0∞\alpha=\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} by

ℒ⁡(α)={a02,a12−a0​a2,a22−a1​a3,a32−a2​a4,…}.\mathcal{L}(\alpha)=\left\{a_{0}^{2},a_{1}^{2}-a_{0}a_{2},a_{2}^{2}-a_{1}a_{3},a_{3}^{2}-a_{2}a_{4},...\right\}.

Hence a sequence α\alpha is log-concave if and only if ℒ⁡(α)\mathcal{L}(\alpha) is nonnegative. A sequence α\alpha is said to be kk-log-concave if ℒj​(α)\mathcal{L}^{j}(\alpha) is a nonnegative sequence for all 0≤j≤k0\leq j\leq k, and infinitely log-concave if it is kk-log-concave for all k≥0k\geq 0.

Following Karlin [19], a finite or infinite matrix is called totally positive if all its minors are nonnegative. The matrix is called totally positive of order rr if its minors of all orders ≤r\leq r are nonnegative. It is easy to see that a nonnegative sequence {ak}k=0∞\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} with no internal zeros is log-concave if and only if its Toeplitz matrix [ai−j]i,j≥0[a_{i-j}]_{i,j\geq 0} is totally positive of order 2. An infinite nonnegative sequence {ak}k=0∞\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is called a Pólya frequency sequence (PF sequence for short) if its Toeplitz matrix [ai−j]i,j≥0[a_{i-j}]_{i,j\geq 0} is totally positive. Thus, a PF sequence is log-concave and hence unimodal. We say that a finite sequence a0,a1,…,ana_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n} is a PF sequence if the corresponding infinite sequence a0,a1,…,an,0,0,…a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},0,0,\ldots is a PF sequence. Call {ak}k=0∞∈PF\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\in\mathrm{PF} if {ak}k=0∞\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is a PF sequence. A fundamental characterization for Pólya frequency sequences states that a sequence {ak}k=0∞\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is a PF sequence if and only if its generating function is analytic in a neighborhood of the origin and has the expansion

∑k≥0ak​xk=c​xm​eσ​x​∏j≥0(1+αj​x)∏j≥0(1−βj​x),\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}x^{k}=cx^{m}e^{\sigma x}\frac{\prod_{j\geq 0}(1+\alpha_{j}x)}{\prod_{j\geq 0}(1-\beta_{j}x)}, (1.1)

where c>0,m∈ℕ,αj,βj,σ≥0c>0,m\in\mathbb{N},\alpha_{j},\beta_{j},\sigma\geq 0, and ∑j≥0(αj+βj)<+∞\sum_{j\geq 0}(\alpha_{j}+\beta_{j})<+\infty (see, for example, [19, p. 412]). Aissen, Schoenberg and Whitney [1] showed that a finite nonnegative sequence {ak}k=0n∈PF\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{n}\in\mathrm{PF} if and only if the generating function of {ak}k=0n\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{n} has only real zeros.

A sequence α={ak}k=0∞\alpha=\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} of nonnegative numbers is log-convex if and only if its Hankel matrix [ai+j]i,j≥0[a_{i+j}]_{i,j\geq 0} is totally positive of order 2. Log-convex sequences are closely related to the Stieltjes moment sequence. We say that α={ak}k=0∞\alpha=\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is a Stieltjes moment sequence (SM sequence for short) if it has the form

ak=∫0∞xk​𝑑μ​(x),a_{k}=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{k}d{\mu(x)},

where μ\mu is a nonnegative measure on [0,+∞)[0,+\infty). The Stieltjes moment problem is one of the classical moment problems and arises naturally in many branches of mathematics [33, 32]. It is well known [30, 32] that the following are equivalent:

  • (i)

    α\alpha is a Stieltjes moment sequence.

  • (ii)

    The Hankel matrix [ai+j]i,j≥0[a_{i+j}]_{i,j\geq 0} is totally positive.

  • (iii)

    For any n≥0n\geq 0, both [ai+j]0≤i,j≤n[a_{i+j}]_{0\leq i,j\leq n} and [ai+j+1]0≤i,j≤n[a_{i+j+1}]_{0\leq i,j\leq n} are positive semidefinite.

The organization of this paper is as follows. In Section 2, we show that for each dd, the row and column sequences in the dd-Hoggatt triangle are infinitely log-concave. In Section 3, we show that the sequences located in a transversal of the dd-Hoggatt triangle are log-concave and the sequences located in a ray are asymptotically log-convex. In addition, we provide a criterion for determining when the sequences located in a ray form an SM sequence. In Sections 4 and 5, we prove the asymptotic normality and total positivity in Hoggatt triangles. In the last section, we consider the log-convexity of the row sums and present a couple of problems.

2 Infinite log-concavity of row and column sequences

Let ⟨n⟩d=(n+d−1d)\left\langle n\right\rangle_{d}=\binom{n+d-1}{d} and ⟨n⟩d!=∏j=1n⟨j⟩d\left\langle n\right\rangle_{d}!=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left\langle j\right\rangle_{d}. Cigler [14] presented the explicit expression of the dd-Hoggatt number,

Hd​(n,k)=⟨n⟩d!⟨k⟩d!​⟨n−k⟩d!=∏j=0d−1(n+jk)(k+jk),0≤k≤nH_{d}(n,k)=\frac{\left\langle n\right\rangle_{d}!}{\left\langle k\right\rangle_{d}!~\left\langle n-k\right\rangle_{d}!}=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\binom{n+j}{k}}{\binom{k+j}{k}},\quad 0\leq k\leq n (2.1)

and Hd​(n,k)=0H_{d}(n,k)=0 for k>nk>n. Using the theory of the multiplier sequence, Dilks derived the following result.

Lemma 2.2 ([15, Theorem 3.8]).

The row generating function of the dd-Hoggatt triangle

Hn,d​(x)=∑k=0nHd​(n,k)​xkH_{n,d}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}H_{d}(n,k)x^{k}

has only real zeros for each d≥1d\geq 1 and n≥0n\geq 0.

Now we turn to the infinite log-concavity of the column sequences of the dd-Hoggatt triangle. Let {ak}k=0∞\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} be a PF sequence interpolated by the polynomial p⁡(x)p(x), i.e., ak=p⁡(k)a_{k}=p(k) for k≥0k\geq 0. Then the generating function of aka_{k} is of the form

∑k=0∞ak​xk=w⁡(x)(1−x)d+1,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k}x^{k}=\frac{w(x)}{(1-x)^{d+1}},

where w⁡(x)w(x) is a polynomial of degree at most dd, see [36, Chapter 4.3]. Since {ak}k=0∞\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is a PF sequence, by (1.1), w⁡(x)w(x) has nonnegative coefficients and only real zeros. Brändén [7] and Brändén and Chasse [8] presented the infinite log-concavity of a PF sequence separately.

Theorem 2.3.

Let {ak}k=0∞\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} be a Pólya frequency sequence.

  1. (i)

    If the polynomial ∑k=0nak​xk\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}x^{k} with nonnegative coefficients has only real zeros, then the sequence a0,a1,…,ana_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{n} is infinitely log-concave.

  2. (ii)

    If there exist p⁡(x)∈ℝ⁡[x]p(x)\in\mathbb{R}[x] and p⁡(−2)=p⁡(−1)=0p(-2)=p(-1)=0 such that ak=p⁡(k)a_{k}=p(k) for each k=0,1,2,…k=0,1,2,\ldots, then {ak}k=0∞\left\{a_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is infinitely log-concave.

The column generating function of Pascal’s triangle is

∑n=0∞(n+kk)​xn=1(1−x)k+1.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{n+k}{k}x^{n}=\frac{1}{(1-x)^{k+1}}.

This implies that {(n+kk)}n=0∞\left\{\binom{n+k}{k}\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is a PF sequence for each kk. The interpolated polynomial

p⁡(x)=(x+kk):=(x+k)​(x+k−1)​…​(x+1)k!p(x)=\binom{x+k}{k}:=\frac{(x+k)(x+k-1)\dots(x+1)}{k!}

with p⁡(−2)=p⁡(−1)=0p(-2)=p(-1)=0 for k≥2k\geq 2. As a corollary, Brändén and Chasse [8] proved that for each k≥0k\geq 0 and i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, ℒi​({(n+kk)}n=0∞)\mathcal{L}^{i}\left(\left\{\binom{n+k}{k}\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\right) is a PF sequence and therefore the column sequence of Pascal’s triangle is infinitely log-concave (the cases k=0k=0 and k=1k=1 trivially hold). Now we show the infinite log-concavity in the dd-Hoggatt triangle.

Theorem 2.4.

The row sequence {Hd​(n,k)}k=0n\left\{H_{d}(n,k)\right\}_{k=0}^{n} and the column sequence of the dd-Hoggatt triangle {Hd​(n+k,k)}n=0∞\left\{H_{d}(n+k,k)\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty} are both infinitely log-concave for each d≥1d\geq 1 and n,k≥0n,k\geq 0.

Proof.

Since the row generating function of dd-Hoggatt triangle Hn,d​(x)H_{n,d}(x) has only real zeros, then the infinite log-concavity of the row sequence follows from Theorem 2.3 (i).

By (2.1), Hd​(n,0)=1H_{d}(n,0)=1 and Hd​(n+1,1)=(n+dd).H_{d}(n+1,1)=\binom{n+d}{d}. The case k=0k=0 trivially holds and the case k=1k=1 reduces to Brändén and Chasse’s result for Pascal’s triangle. For k≥2k\geq 2, we now show that {Hd​(n+k,k)}n=0∞\left\{H_{d}(n+k,k)\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is a PF sequence. Cigler [14, Theorem 4] showed that the column generating function of the dd-Hoggatt triangle has the form

∑n=0∞Hd​(n+k,k)​xn=∑j=0(d−1)​(k−1)N⁡(d,k,j)​xj(1−x)d​k+1,\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}H_{d}(n+k,k)x^{n}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum\limits_{j=0}^{(d-1)(k-1)}N(d,k,j)x^{j}}{(1-x)^{dk+1}},

where N⁡(d,k,j)N(d,k,j) are the Narayana numbers of dimension dd introduced by Sulanke [38]. Chen, Yang and Zhang [11, Theorem 3.1] showed that

∑j=0(d−1)​(k−1)N⁡(d,k,j)​xj\displaystyle\sum\limits_{j=0}^{(d-1)(k-1)}N(d,k,j)x^{j}

has only real nonpositive zeros, which implies that {Hd​(n+k,k)}n=0∞\left\{H_{d}(n+k,k)\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is a PF sequence.

It is easy to see that {Hd​(n+k,k)}n=0∞\left\{H_{d}(n+k,k)\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is interpolated by the polynomial

p⁡(x)=∏j=0d−1(x+k+jk)(k+jk)=∏j=0d−1(x+k+j)​(x+k+j−1)​…​(x+j+1)(k+j)​(k+j−1)​…​(j+1).p(x)=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\binom{x+k+j}{k}}{\binom{k+j}{k}}=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{(x+k+j)(x+k+j-1)\dots(x+j+1)}{(k+j)(k+j-1)\dots(j+1)}.

Clearly, p⁡(−2)=p⁡(−1)=0p(-2)=p(-1)=0. By Theorem 2.3 (ii), {Hd​(n+k,k)}n=0∞\left\{H_{d}(n+k,k)\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is infinitely log-concave. ∎

3 Log-behavior of transversal and ray sequences of Hoggatt triangles

Su and Wang [37] demonstrated that the sequence located in a transversal of Pascal’s triangle is log-concave, and the sequence located in a ray of Pascal’s triangle, not parallel to the column or the diagonal, is asymptotically log-convex, i.e. there exists a nonnegative number mm such that am,am+1,am+2,…a_{m},a_{m+1},a_{m+2},... is log-convex. Yu [41] strengthened these results, confirming the conjectures of Su and Wang [37]. Specifically, Yu established that the transversal sequences of Pascal’s triangle are all PF sequences (see Theorem 6.15); and for the ray sequences of Pascal’s triangle, Yu provided an explicit expression for the index mm, ensuring that the sequence {ai}i=m∞\{a_{i}\}_{i=m}^{\infty} is log-convex. Zhu [45, Proposition 3.7] further extended Yu’s work and showed that the sequence {ai}i=m∞\{a_{i}\}_{i=m}^{\infty} is not merely log-convex but also an SM sequence.

Lemma 3.5 ([45, Theorem 1.5]).

Let n0≥k0≥0n_{0}\geq k_{0}\geq 0 and {p,q,dj,ej}⊆ℝ+\{p,q,d_{j},e_{j}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{+} for j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}. Define the sequence

bi=Γ⁡(n0+i​p+1)Γ⁡(k0+i​q+1)​Γ​((n0−k0)+i⁡(p−q)+1)∏j=0ℓ1i​dj+ej,i=0,1,2,…,b_{i}=\frac{\Gamma{(n_{0}+ip+1)}}{\Gamma{(k_{0}+iq+1)}\Gamma{((n_{0}-k_{0})+i(p-q)+1)}}\prod_{j=0}^{\ell}\frac{1}{id_{j}+e_{j}},~~~i=0,1,2,...,

where Γ⁡(x)\Gamma(x) is the Gamma function. If p>qp>q and (n0+1)​q/p−1≤k0≤(n0+1)​q/p(n_{0}+1)q/p-1\leq k_{0}\leq(n_{0}+1)q/p, then {bi}i=0∞\{b_{i}\}_{i=0}^{\infty} forms a Stieltjes moment sequence.

We generalize these results to the Hoggatt triangles.

Theorem 3.6.

Let n0,k0,p,qn_{0},k_{0},p,q be nonnegative integers with n0≥k0n_{0}\geq k_{0} and d≥1d\geq 1. Define

Ci=Hd(n0+ip,k0+iq),i=0,1,2,….C_{i}=H_{d}(n_{0}+ip,k_{0}+iq),\quad i=0,1,2,\ldots.

Then the following statements hold.

  1. (i)

    If p<qp<q, then {Ci}i=0∞\left\{C_{i}\right\}_{i=0}^{\infty} is log-concave and therefore unimodal;

  2. (ii)

    If p>q>0p>q>0, then {Ci}i=0∞\left\{C_{i}\right\}_{i=0}^{\infty} is asymptotically log-convex;

  3. (iii)

    If p>q>0p>q>0, (d−1)​q≤p(d-1)q\leq p and

    (n0+d)​qp−1≤k0≤(n0+1)​qp,\frac{(n_{0}+d)q}{p}-1\leq k_{0}\leq\frac{(n_{0}+1)q}{p},

    then {Ci}i=0∞\{C_{i}\}_{i=0}^{\infty} forms a Stieltjes moment sequence.

Proof.

(i) Let

⟨nk⟩d:=Hd​(n,k)=⟨n⟩d!⟨k⟩d!​⟨n−k⟩d!.\left\langle\begin{matrix}n\\ k\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}:=H_{d}(n,k)=\frac{\langle n\rangle_{d}!}{\langle k\rangle_{d}!\,\langle n-k\rangle_{d}!}.

To prove that {Ci}i=0∞\left\{C_{i}\right\}_{i=0}^{\infty} is log-concave, it suffices to prove that

Hd​(n+p,k+q)​Hd​(n−p,k−q)≤Hd​(n,k)2H_{d}(n+p,k+q)H_{d}(n-p,k-q)\leq H_{d}(n,k)^{2}

for n≥kn\geq k and p<qp<q. Claim that

Hd​(n+p,k+q)​Hd​(n−p,k−q)=\displaystyle H_{d}(n+p,k+q)H_{d}(n-p,k-q)= Hd​(n+p,n−k)​Hd​(n−p,n−k)\displaystyle H_{d}(n+p,n-k)H_{d}(n-p,n-k)
×Hd​(n−k,q−p)Hd​(n−k+q−p,q−p)​Hd​(k−p,q−p)Hd​(k+q,q−p).\displaystyle\times\frac{H_{d}(n-k,q-p)}{H_{d}(n-k+q-p,q-p)}\frac{H_{d}(k-p,q-p)}{H_{d}(k+q,q-p)}.

This follows from

⟨n+pk+q⟩d​⟨n−pk−q⟩d=\displaystyle\left\langle\begin{matrix}n+p\\ k+q\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}\left\langle\begin{matrix}n-p\\ k-q\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}= ⟨n+p⟩d!​⟨n−p⟩d!⟨k+q⟩d!​⟨n+p−k−q⟩d!​⟨k−q⟩d!​⟨n−p−k+q⟩d!\displaystyle\frac{\left\langle n+p\right\rangle_{d}!\left\langle n-p\right\rangle_{d}!}{\left\langle k+q\right\rangle_{d}!\left\langle n+p-k-q\right\rangle_{d}!\left\langle k-q\right\rangle_{d}!\left\langle n-p-k+q\right\rangle_{d}!}
=\displaystyle= ⟨n+pn−k⟩d​⟨n−pn−k⟩d​⟨n−kq−p⟩d⟨n−k+q−pq−p⟩d​⟨k−pq−p⟩d⟨k+qq−p⟩d.\displaystyle\left\langle\begin{matrix}n+p\\ n-k\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}\left\langle\begin{matrix}n-p\\ n-k\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}\frac{\left\langle\begin{matrix}n-k\\ q-p\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}}{\left\langle\begin{matrix}n-k+q-p\\ q-p\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}}\frac{\left\langle\begin{matrix}k-p\\ q-p\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}}{\left\langle\begin{matrix}k+q\\ q-p\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}}.

Combining the log-concavity of the column sequence (Theorem 2.4 (ii)) and the symmetry Hd​(n,k)=Hd​(n,n−k)H_{d}(n,k)=H_{d}(n,n-k), we have

Hd​(n+p,n−k)​Hd​(n−p,n−k)≤Hd​(n,n−k)2=Hd​(n,k)2.H_{d}(n+p,n-k)H_{d}(n-p,n-k)\leq H_{d}(n,n-k)^{2}=H_{d}(n,k)^{2}.

Moreover, the column sequence is increasing, since

⟨n+1k⟩d/⟨nk⟩d=⟨n+1⟩d⟨n+1−k⟩d≥1.{\left\langle\begin{matrix}n+1\\ k\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}}\bigg/{\left\langle\begin{matrix}n\\ k\end{matrix}\right\rangle_{d}}=\frac{\left\langle n+1\right\rangle_{d}}{\left\langle n+1-k\right\rangle_{d}}\geq 1.

Thus we obtain that

Hd​(n−k,q−p)Hd​(n−k+q−p,q−p)​Hd​(k−p,q−p)Hd​(k+q,q−p)≤1.\frac{H_{d}(n-k,q-p)}{H_{d}(n-k+q-p,q-p)}\frac{H_{d}(k-p,q-p)}{H_{d}(k+q,q-p)}\leq 1.

Hence,

Hd​(n+p,k+q)​Hd​(n−p,k−q)≤Hd​(n,k)2.H_{d}(n+p,k+q)H_{d}(n-p,k-q)\leq H_{d}(n,k)^{2}.

(ii) Let n=n0+i​p,n=n_{0}+ip, and k=k0+i​qk=k_{0}+iq. It suffices to show that

Δ⁡(k):=Hd​(n+p,k+q)​Hd​(n−p,k−q)Hd​(n,k)2≥1\Delta(k):=\frac{H_{d}(n+p,k+q)H_{d}(n-p,k-q)}{H_{d}(n,k)^{2}}\geq 1

for all sufficiently large kk, where n=n0+p​k−k0qn=n_{0}+p\frac{k-k_{0}}{q} and p>q>0p>q>0. By (2.1),

Hd​(n,k)=∏j=0d−1(n+jk)(k+jk)=∏j=0d−1(n+j)!​j!(k+j)!​(n−k+j)!.H_{d}(n,k)=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\binom{n+j}{k}}{\binom{k+j}{k}}=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{(n+j)!j!}{(k+j)!(n-k+j)!}.

Hence

Claim that if {ak}k=0∞\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} and {bk}k=0∞\{b_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} are two Stieltjes moment sequences, then so is {ak​bk}k=0∞\{a_{k}b_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty}. The sequence {ak}k=0∞\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} (resp. {bk}k=0∞\{b_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty}) is an SM sequence if and only if Hankel matrices [ai+j]i,j=0n[a_{i+j}]_{i,j=0}^{n} and [ai+j+1]i,j=0n[a_{i+j+1}]_{i,j=0}^{n} (resp. [bi+j]i,j=0n[b_{i+j}]_{i,j=0}^{n} and [bi+j+1]i,j=0n[b_{i+j+1}]_{i,j=0}^{n}) are positive semidefinite. The famous Schur product theorem states that the Hadamard product of two positive semidefinite matrices is still positive semidefinite, see [18, Theorem 7.5.3]. Then [ai+j​bi+j]i,j=0n[a_{i+j}b_{i+j}]_{i,j=0}^{n} and [ai+j+1​bi+j+1]i,j=0n[a_{i+j+1}b_{i+j+1}]_{i,j=0}^{n} are still positive semidefinite. Thus {ak​bk}k=0∞\{a_{k}b_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is an SM sequence. Hence, the Hadamard product of two SM sequences is still an SM sequence. Therefore, {Ci}i=0∞\left\{C_{i}\right\}_{i=0}^{\infty} is an SM sequence. ∎

4 Asymptotic normality in Hoggatt triangles

The normal distribution consists of a symmetric bell-shaped curve with a downward-sloping curve on each side of the mode. Let a⁡(n,k)a(n,k) be a double-indexed sequence of nonnegative numbers. In combinatorics, when a⁡(n,k)a(n,k) is unimodal with respect to kk for sufficiently large nn, it is natural to consider the asymptotic normality.

Let XnX_{n} be a random variable, and let

p⁡(n,k)=P⁡(Xn=k)=a⁡(n,k)∑ja⁡(n,j)p(n,k)=P(X_{n}=k)=\frac{a(n,k)}{\sum_{j}a(n,j)}

denote the normalized probabilities. Following Bender [3], we say that the sequence a⁡(n,k)a(n,k) (or equivalently, XnX_{n}) is asymptotically normal by a central limit theorem, if

limn→∞supx∈ℝ|∑k≤μn+x​σnp⁡(n,k)−12​π​∫−∞xe−t22​𝑑t|=0,\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\sum_{k\leq\mu_{n}+x\sigma_{n}}p(n,k)-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{x}e^{\frac{-t^{2}}{2}}dt\right|=0, (4.1)

where μn\mu_{n} and σn2\sigma_{n}^{2} are the mean and variance of a⁡(n,k)a(n,k), respectively.

The study of limit distributions of combinatorial sequences is useful for precisely predicting the properties of large structured combinatorial configurations. Many well-known combinatorial sequences enjoy central and local limit theorems. For example, the famous de Moivre-Laplace theorem states that the binomial coefficients H1​(n,k)H_{1}(n,k) are asymptotically normal (by central and local limit theorems). We refer the reader to [9] for other examples. Chen et al. [10] showed that the Narayana numbers H2​(n,k)H_{2}(n,k) are asymptotically normal and Zhao [43] showed that the refined Baxter numbers H3​(n,k)H_{3}(n,k) are asymptotically normal. Both proofs rely on the fact that the row generating functions have only real zeros. Here we prove the general result that the dd-Hoggatt numbers Hd​(n,k)H_{d}(n,k) are asymptotically normal by direct approximations. Throughout this section, the symbols OO, oo and ∼\sim have their usual meaning:

f⁡(n)=O⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=O(g(n)) means f⁡(n)/g⁡(n)f(n)/g(n) is bounded as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty;

f⁡(n)=o⁡(g⁡(n))f(n)=o(g(n)) means f⁡(n)/g⁡(n)→0f(n)/g(n)\rightarrow 0 as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty;

f⁡(n)∼g⁡(n)f(n)\sim g(n) means f⁡(n)/g⁡(n)→1f(n)/g(n)\rightarrow 1 as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty.

Suppose that a⁡(n,k)∼b⁡(n,k)a(n,k)\sim b(n,k). Note that it does not imply

∑ka⁡(n,k)∼∑kb⁡(n,k).\sum_{k}a(n,k)\sim\sum_{k}b(n,k).

We say that a⁡(n,k)∼b⁡(n,k)a(n,k)\sim b(n,k) uniformly for k∈S⁡(n)k\in S(n) provided a⁡(n,k)=b⁡(n,k)​(1+o⁡(1))a(n,k)=b(n,k)(1+o(1)) whenever k∈S⁡(n)k\in S(n), where the constant in the oo is independent of kk. In this case we can write

∑k∈S⁡(n)a⁡(n,k)=∑k∈S⁡(n)b⁡(n,k)+o⁡(∑k∈S⁡(n)|b⁡(n,k)|)\sum_{k\in S(n)}a(n,k)=\sum_{k\in S(n)}b(n,k)+o\left(\sum_{k\in S(n)}|b(n,k)|\right)

and in particular

∑k∈S⁡(n)a⁡(n,k)∼∑k∈S⁡(n)b⁡(n,k).\sum_{k\in S(n)}a(n,k)\sim\sum_{k\in S(n)}b(n,k).

See [4, p. 487] for instance. The following proof is motivated by Bender [4].

Theorem 4.8.

For each d≥1d\geq 1, the dd-Hoggatt numbers Hd​(n,k)H_{d}(n,k) are asymptotically normal, with the mean μn=n2\mu_{n}=\frac{n}{2} and variance σn2∼n4​d\sigma_{n}^{2}\sim\frac{n}{4d}.

Proof.

By the symmetry

Hd​(n,k)=Hd​(n,n−k),H_{d}(n,k)=H_{d}(n,n-k),

Recall that

log⁡(x+r)=log⁡x+rx−r22​x2+O⁡(r3x3).\log(x+r)=\log x+\frac{r}{x}-\frac{r^{2}}{2x^{2}}+O\left(\frac{r^{3}}{x^{3}}\right).

By

log⁡Am,d​(s)Am,d​(0)=−d​s2m+O⁡(s2m2)+O⁡(s2m2+s4m3)=−d​s2m+O⁡(s2m2+s4m3).\log\frac{A_{m,d}(s)}{A_{m,d}(0)}=-\frac{ds^{2}}{m}+O\left(\frac{s^{2}}{m^{2}}\right)+O\left(\frac{s^{2}}{m^{2}}+\frac{s^{4}}{m^{3}}\right)=-\frac{ds^{2}}{m}+O\left(\frac{s^{2}}{m^{2}}+\frac{s^{4}}{m^{3}}\right).

In particular,

Since n=2​mn=2m, we have

5 Total positivity of Hoggatt triangles

The purpose of this section is to prove the total positivity of the Hoggatt triangles. It is folklore [30] that Pascal’s triangle [H1​(n,k)]n,k≥0[H_{1}(n,k)]_{n,k\geq 0} is totally positive. Wang and Yang [40] showed that the Narayana triangle [H2​(n,k)]n,k≥0[H_{2}(n,k)]_{n,k\geq 0} and the Narayana square [H2​(n+k,k)]n,k≥0[H_{2}(n+k,k)]_{n,k\geq 0} are totally positive. Inspired by Wang and Yang, we consider the total positivity of the dd-Hoggatt triangle.

A sequence T={γk}k=0∞T=\{\gamma_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} of real numbers is called a multiplier sequence if, whenever the real polynomial p⁡(x)=∑k=0nak​xkp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}x^{k} has only real zeros, the polynomial T⁡[p⁡(x)]=∑k=0nγk​ak​xkT[p(x)]=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\gamma_{k}a_{k}x^{k} also has only real zeros. By the definition of multiplier sequence, we can obtain the following result.

Lemma 5.9.

Let {γk}k=0∞\left\{\gamma_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} and {τk}k=0∞\left\{\tau_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} be multiplier sequences. Then so is {γk​τk}k=0∞\left\{\gamma_{k}\tau_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty}.

Let φ⁡(x)=∑k=0∞γkk!​xk\varphi(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\gamma_{k}}{k!}x^{k}. Then the sequence {γk}k=0∞\{\gamma_{k}\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is a multiplier sequence if and only if either φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) or φ⁡(−x)\varphi(-x) defines an entire function that can be written as

c​xm​eσ​x​∏j=1∞(1+αj​x),cx^{m}e^{\sigma x}\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}(1+\alpha_{j}x), (5.1)

where c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, αj≥0\alpha_{j}\geq 0 for all j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}, and ∑j≥1αj<∞\sum_{j\geq 1}\alpha_{j}<\infty (see [21] for instance). Comparing (5.1) with the generating function of PF sequences (1.1), the following result is immediate.

Lemma 5.10.

If a sequence {γk}k=0∞\left\{\gamma_{k}\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} of nonnegative numbers is a multiplier sequence, then {γk/k!}k=0∞\left\{\gamma_{k}/k!\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is a Pólya frequency sequence.

Let A=[an,k]n,k≥0A=[a_{n,k}]_{n,k\geq 0} and B=[bn,k]n,k≥0B=[b_{n,k}]_{n,k\geq 0} be two matrices. If there exist positive numbers xnx_{n} and yky_{k} such that bn,k=xn​yk​an,kb_{n,k}=x_{n}y_{k}a_{n,k} for all nn and kk, then we denote an,k≃bn,ka_{n,k}\simeq b_{n,k} and A≃BA\simeq B.

Lemma 5.11 ([40, Proposition 2.1]).

Suppose that A≃BA\simeq B. Then the matrix AA is totally positive if and only if the matrix BB is totally positive.

We obtain the following results.

Theorem 5.12.

For each d≥1d\geq 1, both the dd-Hoggatt triangle

Hd=[Hd​(n,k)]n,k≥0H_{d}=[H_{d}(n,k)]_{n,k\geq 0}

and the dd-Hoggatt square

Hd⌜=[Hd​(n+k,k)]n,k≥0H_{d}^{\ulcorner}=[H_{d}(n+k,k)]_{n,k\geq 0}

are totally positive.

Proof.

Note that 1/r!=01/r!=0 when r<0r<0. By (2.1),

Hd​(n,k)=∏j=0d−1(n+jk)(k+jk).H_{d}(n,k)=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\binom{n+j}{k}}{\binom{k+j}{k}}.

Since (k+jk)\binom{k+j}{k} depends only on kk, multiplying the kk-th column by the positive number ∏j=0d−1(k+jk)\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\binom{k+j}{k} does not affect total positivity. Hence

Hd​(n,k)≃∏j=0d−1(n+jk).H_{d}(n,k)\simeq\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\binom{n+j}{k}.

Furthermore,

(n+jk)=(n+j)!k!​(n−k+j)!≃1(n−k+j)!,\binom{n+j}{k}=\frac{(n+j)!}{k!(n-k+j)!}\simeq\frac{1}{(n-k+j)!},

where the factor (n+j)!(n+j)! depends only on nn, and k!k! depends only on kk. Therefore

Hd​(n,k)≃∏j=0d−11(n−k+j)!.H_{d}(n,k)\simeq\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{1}{(n-k+j)!}.

Writing N=n−kN=n-k, we have

∏j=0d−11(N+j)!≃1N!​∏j=2d1(j)N.\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{1}{(N+j)!}\simeq\frac{1}{N!}\prod_{j=2}^{d}\frac{1}{(j)_{N}}.

Thus the total positivity of HdH_{d} is equivalent to that of the Toeplitz matrix generated by the sequence

αn=1n!​∏j=2d1(j)n,n≥0.\alpha_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}\prod_{j=2}^{d}\frac{1}{(j)_{n}},\qquad n\geq 0.

A classic result [21, p.341] of Laguerre on multiplier sequences states that for any t>0t>0, the sequence {1/(t)n}n=0∞\left\{{1}/{(t)_{n}}\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is a multiplier sequence. It follows by Lemma 5.9 that the Hadamard product sequence

{∏j=2d1/(j)n}n=0∞\left\{\prod_{j=2}^{d}{1}/{(j)_{n}}\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty}

is a multiplier sequence. Thus, the sequence {1n!​∏j=2d1(j)n}n=0∞\left\{\frac{1}{n!}\prod_{j=2}^{d}\frac{1}{(j)_{n}}\right\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is a PF sequence by Lemma 5.10, which implies that the corresponding Toeplitz matrix

[1(n−k)!​∏j=2d1(j)n−k]n,k≥0\left[\frac{1}{(n-k)!}\prod_{j=2}^{d}\frac{1}{(j)_{n-k}}\right]_{n,k\geq 0}

is TP. By Lemma 5.11, Hd=[Hd​(n,k)]n,k≥0H_{d}=[H_{d}(n,k)]_{n,k\geq 0} is totally positive.

Next we prove the total positivity of Hd⌜H_{d}^{\ulcorner}. Again by (2.1),

Hd​(n+k,k)=∏j=0d−1(n+k+jk)(k+jk).H_{d}(n+k,k)=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\frac{\binom{n+k+j}{k}}{\binom{k+j}{k}}.

Removing row and column factors, we get

Hd​(n+k,k)≃∏j=0d−1(n+k+j)!.H_{d}(n+k,k)\simeq\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(n+k+j)!.

The sequence {m!}m=0∞\{m!\}_{m=0}^{\infty} is an SM sequence since m!=∫0∞xm​e−x​𝑑x.m!=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{m}e^{-x}\,dx. The total positivity of [(n+k)!]n,k≥0[(n+k)!]_{n,k\geq 0} implies that of [(n+k+j)!]n,k≥0[(n+k+j)!]_{n,k\geq 0} for j≥0j\geq 0, since [(n+k+j)!]n,k≥0[(n+k+j)!]_{n,k\geq 0} is a submatrix of [(n+k)!]n,k≥0[(n+k)!]_{n,k\geq 0}, and the submatrix of a totally positive matrix is still totally positive. Thus the sequence {(k+j)!}k=0∞\left\{(k+j)!\right\}_{k=0}^{\infty} is an SM sequence. The Hadamard product of two SM sequences is still an SM sequence, see the proof of Theorem 3.6 (iii). Hence, the Hankel matrix

[∏j=0d−1(n+k+j)!]n,k≥0\left[\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(n+k+j)!\right]_{n,k\geq 0}

is totally positive. Thus we obtain that Hd⌜=[Hd​(n+k,k)]n,k≥0H_{d}^{\ulcorner}=[H_{d}(n+k,k)]_{n,k\geq 0} is totally positive. ∎

Let

Hn,d=Hn,d​(1)=∑k=0nHd​(n,k)H_{n,d}=H_{n,d}(1)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}H_{d}(n,k)

be the nn-th row sum of the dd-Hoggatt triangle. It is easy to see that Hn,1=2nH_{n,1}=2^{n} and Hn,2=1n+2​(2​n+2n+1)H_{n,2}=\frac{1}{n+2}\binom{2n+2}{n+1} are log-convex. Consider the Baxter numbers

Bn=Hn,3=∑k=0nH3​(n,k)=∑k=0n(nk)​(n+1k)​(n+2k)(k+1k)​(k+2k).B_{n}=H_{n,3}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}H_{3}(n,k)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\binom{n}{k}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+2}{k}}{\binom{k+1}{k}\binom{k+2}{k}}.

Bouvel et al. [5] investigated the combinatorial interpretations of the Baxter numbers BnB_{n}. It is natural to consider the log-convexity of the sequence of row sums of the Hoggatt triangles. Similarly, we derive that the row sum of the 44-Hoggatt matrix Hn,4=∑k=0nH4​(n,k)H_{n,4}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}H_{4}(n,k) satisfies the three-term recurrence

(n+4)​(n+5)​(n+6)​(n+7)​Hn+1,4=\displaystyle(n+4)(n+5)(n+6)(n+7)H_{n+1,4}= 6​(n+2)​(n+4)​(n+5)​(7+2​n)​Hn,4\displaystyle 6(n+2)(n+4)(n+5)(7+2n)H_{n,4}
+4​n​(n+1)​(11+4​n)​(13+4​n)​Hn−1,4\displaystyle+4n(n+1)(11+4n)(13+4n)H_{n-1,4}

with H0,4=1,H1,4=2H_{0,4}=1,H_{1,4}=2, see [34, A005362] for instance. The log-convexity of {Hn,4}n=0∞\{H_{n,4}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} can be obtained similarly.

Unfortunately for d≥5d\geq 5, we have not found the three-term recurrence of the row sum. Numerical results suggest that the sequence {Hn,d}n=0∞\{H_{n,d}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is log-convex. Kotěšovec [20] considered the asymptotic formula for the numbers Hn,d​(n≥1)H_{n,d}~(n\geq 1),

Hn,d∼2−12+d⁡(−12+d+n)​n−d22​nd​π1−d2​G​(1+d),\displaystyle H_{n,d}\sim 2^{-\frac{1}{2}+d(-\frac{1}{2}+d+n)}n^{-\frac{d^{2}}{2}}\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}}{\pi}^{\frac{1-d}{2}}G(1+d),

where G⁡(n)G(n) is the Barnes G-function. This shows that the sequence of {Hn,d}n=0∞\{H_{n,d}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is asymptotically log-convex for d≥5d\geq 5. Note that

2n=∫0∞xn​δ​(x−2)​𝑑xand1n+1​(2​nn)=∫0∞xn​(12​π​4−xx)​I(0,4]​(x)​𝑑x2^{n}=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{n}\delta(x-2)dx\quad\textrm{and}\quad\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{n}\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{4-x}{x}}\right)I_{(0,4]}(x)dx (6.2)

where δ⁡(x)\delta(x) is the Dirac delta function and IAI_{A} is the indicator function of the set AA, see [23, Eq.(1.2)] and [24, Eq.(3)] respectively. Hence {Hn,1}n=0∞\{H_{n,1}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} and {Hn,2}n=0∞\{H_{n,2}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} are both SM sequences. (Actually the second equation in (6.2) yields that {Hn−1,2}n=0∞\{H_{n-1,2}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} is an SM sequence and the shifted sequence of an SM sequence is still an SM sequence.) It is natural to consider the SM property of {Hn,d}n=0∞\{H_{n,d}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} for d≥3d\geq 3.

The polynomial sequence {fn​(x)}n≥0\{f_{n}(x)\}_{n\geq 0} is called xx-log-convex if fn−1​(x)​fn+1​(x)−fn​(x)2f_{n-1}(x)f_{n+1}(x)-f_{n}(x)^{2} has nonnegative coefficients for all n≥1n\geq 1. Clearly the xx-log-convexity of Hn,d​(x)H_{n,d}(x) implies the log-convexity of Hn,dH_{n,d}. The xx-log-convexity of the Narayana polynomial Hn,2​(x)H_{n,2}(x) was conjectured by Liu and Wang [25], and solved by Chen, Yang and Wang [12] and Zhu [44]. Zhu [46] studied xx-log-convexity of the row-generating polynomials of certain matrices. An interesting problem is to show the xx-log-convexity of Hn,d​(x)H_{n,d}(x) for d≥3d\geq 3.

Yu [41] strengthened Theorem 3.6 (i) on Pascal’s triangle.

Theorem 6.15 ([41, Section 2]).

Let n0,k0,p,qn_{0},k_{0},p,q be integers such that n0≥k0≥0,q>p>0,n_{0}\geq k_{0}\geq 0,q>p>0, and k0<qk_{0}<q. Define Ci=(n0+i​pk0+i​q)C_{i}=\binom{n_{0}+ip}{k_{0}+iq}, i=0,1,2,….i=0,1,2,\dots. Then the polynomial ∑i≥0Ci​xi\sum_{i\geq 0}C_{i}x^{i} has only real zeros.

It might be of interest to ask whether these results can be generalized to the dd-Hoggatt triangle for d≥2d\geq 2.
